title: Treasury Bills vs Notes vs Bonds: How to Choose
metaDescription: Treasury bills vs notes vs bonds compared: see how maturities, discount vs coupon payments, price risk, and tax rules determine which Treasury to buy.

h1: Treasury Bills vs Notes vs Bonds: Which Fits Your Timeline?
introText:
Treasury bills mature in 4 to 52 weeks and sell at a discount, while Treasury notes and bonds run from 2 to 30 years and pay cash interest every six months. At ModernWallet, we evaluate cash and fixed-income options by matching maturities to withdrawal goals so savers avoid forced early sales. All three options share direct U.S. government backing, a $100 purchase minimum, and an exemption from state income tax.

The choice comes down to when you need your money back and how much price risk you can accept if you sell early. Shorter terms limit your exposure to secondary market price drops, while longer terms lock in a coupon rate across market cycles.

verdict: Choose Treasury bills if you need your money within the next 12 months, want minimal price risk, or prefer rolling short-term cash without committing to multi-year locks. Choose Treasury notes or bonds if you want steady income every six months and desire a predictable coupon rate for 2 to 30 years. Neither choice works well if you might need immediate cash tomorrow morning without waiting for settlement. In that situation, keep funds in an accessible deposit vehicle like those in our [Best Money Market Accounts](/roundup/best-money-market-accounts/) guide. Our recommendation flips toward Treasury bills if you expect you may need to sell before maturity, because a note or bond sold before maturity can fetch less than face value if interest rates have risen since you bought it.

sections.heading: Treasury Bills vs Notes vs Bonds at a Glance
sections.content:
Treasury bills, notes, and bonds differ in two ways: how long they run and how they pay you. [Treasury bills](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/treasury-bills/) cover terms from 4 to 52 weeks. They are zero-coupon instruments sold at a discount or at par, paying their full face value when the bill reaches its maturity date.

[Treasury notes](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/treasury-notes/) span intermediate durations of 2, 3, 5, 7, or 10 years. [Treasury bonds](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/treasury-bonds/) extend across long horizons of 20 or 30 years. Both notes and bonds pay a fixed interest rate every six months until maturity, when the government returns the full par principal.

All three instruments carry the direct backing of the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. They require a modest $100 entry point through [TreasuryDirect](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/) or a brokerage account. If you want to compare fixed bank deposits against government paper, review our breakdown on [CD vs Treasury Bill](/compare/cd-vs-treasury-bill/).

sections.heading: How Each Security Pays Returns to Investors
sections.content:
Treasury bills generate income through an upfront purchase discount, whereas Treasury notes and bonds pay periodic cash coupons twice per year. When you purchase a bill, you generally pay less than its stated face value. For instance, using made-up round numbers, you might buy a $1,000 bill for $970, and the U.S. Treasury delivers the full $1,000 to your account upon maturity.

Treasury notes and bonds operate under fixed semiannual payment schedules. When you buy a 10-year note or a 30-year bond at auction, you lock in a stated coupon rate. Every six months, the government deposits that interest payment directly into your designated bank account or brokerage sweep fund.

This structural distinction changes cash flow planning. A retiree who wants a payment every six months might prefer note coupons. A saver closing on a home in eight months can buy a 26-week bill and have the full face value back before closing.

sections.heading: Maturity Horizons and Secondary Market Price Risk
sections.content:
Holding any Treasury security to maturity guarantees return of your full face value plus all stated interest, but selling early exposes you to market price risk. As detailed by [Investor.gov](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/bonds-or-fixed-income-products/bonds), secondary market bond prices drop when interest rates rise. That dynamic means you might have to sell at a discount if you cannot wait for the maturity date.

Maturity length dictates the severity of price swings. A 4-week or 13-week Treasury bill experiences minimal market price fluctuation because its scheduled maturity date sits right around the corner.

A 10-year note or 30-year bond has years of fixed coupons left, so its market price falls further than a bill's when interest rates rise. For broader asset classes across multi-year horizons, read our analysis on [Stocks vs Bonds](/compare/stocks-vs-bonds/) to evaluate duration risk against equity volatility.

sections.heading: Reinvestment and Rate Locks
sections.content:
Treasury bills offer flexible automated rolling for cash management, whereas notes and bonds deliver long-term certainty by locking your interest rate for years. Savers using short bills face reinvestment risk. That occurs when a bill matures and newly issued replacement bills offer lower yields than the original purchase.

TreasuryDirect provides tools for automated bill purchases. You can schedule automatic reinvestment at purchase or up to four business days before maturity. A bill automatically reinvests into the same term length, such as a 52-week bill rolling once or a 4-week bill reinvesting up to 25 consecutive times.

Notes and bonds eliminate the need to constantly monitor auction schedules. Once you purchase a 7-year note or a 20-year bond, your interest rate remains locked for the entire multi-year holding period. You avoid rolling overhead, though you surrender higher short-term rates if market yields rise.

sections.heading: Taxes on Bills, Notes, and Bonds
sections.content:
Bills, notes, and bonds get the same tax treatment: the IRS taxes the interest as ordinary income, and states and cities cannot tax it. Under [IRS Publication 550](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550), interest earned on all marketable Treasury securities is exempt from state and local income taxes. For savers residing in high-income-tax states, this exemption provides a noticeable advantage over fully taxable corporate paper or standard bank deposits.

Custodians and TreasuryDirect report your annual Treasury earnings on [Form 1099-INT](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099int) box 3, titled Interest on U.S. Savings Bonds and Treasury Obligations. You report it on your federal return, and your state cannot tax it.

The timing of your tax liability varies slightly based on how returns are paid. Notes and bonds produce taxable coupon income in the calendar year payments are received. A discount Treasury bill bought in late autumn that matures the following February generates interest income reportable on your taxes in the year of maturity. For the full tax rules, see our guide on [Are Treasury Bills Taxable](/guides/are-treasury-bills-taxable/).

sections.heading: Purchasing Channels and Early Liquidity Rules
sections.content:
Individual investors can buy Treasury securities directly from the federal government or through commercial brokerage firms. TreasuryDirect permits non-competitive bids only, guaranteeing you receive the security in the amount requested at the final auction clearing yield. To learn the exact account setup steps, consult our tutorial on [How to Buy Treasury Bills](/guides/how-to-buy-treasury-bills/).

A brokerage account adds two things TreasuryDirect does not offer: competitive bids and the ability to sell before maturity. Online Treasury trades at [Charles Schwab](https://www.schwab.com/pricing) and [Fidelity](https://www.fidelity.com/trading/commissions-margin-rates) carry zero-dollar commission fees for auction and secondary orders, though representative-assisted orders carry service fees of $25 at Schwab and $19.95 at Fidelity.

If you hold a Treasury security in TreasuryDirect and decide to sell prior to maturity, you must hold the asset for at least 45 days before you can transfer it to a bank, broker, or dealer to execute the sale. If you anticipate needing liquidity before maturity arrives, check our list of the [Best Brokers for Treasury Bonds](/roundup/best-brokers-for-treasury-bonds/) to hold your positions inside a brokerage from day one.

sections.heading: Other Treasury Types: TIPS and Floating Rate Notes
sections.content:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury issues two additional marketable debt instruments designed for specialized inflation and interest rate environments. [Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS)](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/tips/) are issued in terms of 5, 10, or 30 years. TIPS pay a fixed rate twice yearly on a principal value that adjusts upward or downward with inflation, and at maturity, the government pays the greater of the adjusted or original principal.

[Floating Rate Notes (FRNs)](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/floating-rate-notes/) address short-term interest rate shifts over a two-year maturity window. An FRN pays interest quarterly, with payments tied to the discount rate of the most recent 13-week Treasury bill auction plus an established spread.

Investors who want inflation protection often compare TIPS against non-marketable savings bonds. If you are balancing inflation hedges against fixed-coupon notes, consult our direct comparison of [I Bonds vs TIPS](/compare/i-bonds-vs-tips/) for an in-depth breakdown.

sections.heading: How to Choose Based on Your Time Horizon
sections.content:
Matching your target spending date to the maturity of your Treasury security prevents forced sales and locks in expected returns. If you have an upcoming expense due in six months, such as tuition or property taxes, a 26-week bill matches your cash flow needs without exposing your principal to secondary market swings.

Intermediate goals spanning several years call for Treasury notes. A saver setting aside cash for a home down payment four years from now can buy a 3-year note, which pays a coupon every six months and returns the principal a year before the purchase.

Long-term wealth preservation and permanent fixed-income portfolios benefit most from Treasury bonds. Holding a 20-year or 30-year bond fixes your coupon income for decades. Assess your required access date before placing an order to select the correct Treasury vehicle.

faqs.question: Are Treasury bills and bonds the same thing?
faqs.answer: No, Treasury bills and bonds differ in maturity lengths and payment methods. Treasury bills mature in 52 weeks or less and sell at a discount with no coupon payments. Treasury bonds mature in 20 or 30 years and distribute fixed cash interest payments every six months. Both share identical federal government backing and state tax exemptions.

faqs.question: Which is better, T-bills or Treasury bonds?
faqs.answer: Neither security is universally better because the right choice depends on your time horizon and tolerance for market price risk. Treasury bills fit investors who need their money within 12 months and want to avoid secondary market price drops. Treasury bonds work better for investors seeking steady, predictable income locked across a multi-decade horizon.

faqs.question: Do Treasury bills pay interest?
faqs.answer: Yes, Treasury bills pay interest, but they deliver it through a purchase price discount rather than periodic coupon checks. You pay less than the stated face value upfront, and the federal government pays the full face value at maturity. The difference between what you paid and what you receive at maturity constitutes your earned interest income.

faqs.question: What is the minimum to buy a Treasury note?
faqs.answer: The minimum purchase requirement for a Treasury note is $100. Investors can purchase additional amounts in increments of $100. This identical $100 minimum threshold applies whether you buy Treasury notes, bills, or bonds through TreasuryDirect or a participating brokerage firm.

faqs.question: Can you lose money on Treasury bonds?
faqs.answer: You will not lose money on a Treasury bond if you hold it until its scheduled maturity date, because the U.S. government guarantees full return of face value. However, if you sell a Treasury bond on the secondary market before maturity, you can lose principal if interest rates have increased since your initial purchase date.

faqs.question: Are Treasury notes taxable by my state?
faqs.answer: No, interest earned on Treasury notes is completely exempt from all state and local income taxes under federal law. You must still report and pay federal income tax on your earnings. This statutory state exemption applies across all marketable Treasury issues, including bills, notes, and bonds.
